title: Taped Mouth Performance Differnces Study - Investigating changes in physical performance with prevented mouth breathing
summary:
Mouth taping is a new training method that is increasingly being used in the training of competitive athletes and is gaining popularity and imitation through its dissemination in various social media channels. Athletes train with their mouths taped shut. This means that only nasal breathing can be practiced during the sporting activity.

In the context of competitive sports, insufficient data exist to date on the effect of this method on physiological parameters during exercise. In addition, it is not known how mouth taping affects cardiopulmonary performance and parameters relevant to training. Established training methods for this popular trend have not yet been derived.
The rationale behind the training method is presumably based on a restriction of the respiratory capacity and thus a restriction of the oxygen uptake capacity under athletic stress. This is expected to result in a higher training stimulus at the same sporting intensity in order to achieve better adaptation mechanisms and an increase in performance, especially in endurance performance.
Typically, athletes switch from nasal breathing practiced at rest to forced mouth and nose breathing under increasing athletic stress. The larger airway opening can generate a higher respiratory minute volume, which is better able to meet the higher oxygen demand due to sport.
However, it is unclear whether the parameters relevant to performance physiology and training really change as a result of prevented mouth breathing, and if so, in what way. Conceivable approaches would be a restriction of the maximum oxygen uptake capacity (VO2max) caused by the prevented mouth breathing, which leads to a relative oxygen reduction in the tissues under stress (e.g. muscles), similar to what one tries to achieve in altitude training.
To the best of our knowledge, there have been no scientific studies on this topic in a collective of competitive athletes. Furthermore, it is unclear whether and how the subjective performance perception of athletes with taped mouths differs compared to the normal situation (without prevented mouth breathing).
In a monocentric cross-over study we want to objectify the physical performance of competitive and recreational athletes with and without a taped mouth according to standardized procedures for performance diagnostics (spiroergometry) in order to draw conclusions about possible changes in performance- and training-relevant parameters (maximum power in watts, VO2max and other secondary parameters).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Cohort 1):
•    Competitive sports at national and/or international level (e.g., participation in national leagues, state/national squad status)
•    Training at least 3 times a week
•    Written informed consent available

Cohort 2): 
•    Regular sporting activity with a training workload of at least 3 times per week
•    Written informed consent available
Exclusion criteria:
- Ineligibility for competitive sports due to illness/injury
- Nasal airway obstruction
- Diseases of the respiratory tract (e.g. bronchial asthma, COPD)
- Use of medications with respiratory modulating effects (e.g., xylometazoline-containing nasal spray, inhaled bronchodilators, or other agents with comparable effects)
- Pregnancy and breastfeeding
- Nicotine use
